# Dual roles of host N-glycosylation in enteropathogenic Escherichia coli infection

**Authors:** Klil Cohen Yaron; Yaakov Socol; Noam Yedidi; Michal Bejerano-Sagie; Miriam Ravins; Shira Fine-Leebhoff; Liron Birimberg-Schwartz; Myriam Grunewald; Karthik Hullahalli; Afonso de Sousa Vieira; Matthew K. Waldor; Sina Bartfeld; Sigal Ben-Yehuda; Ilan Rosenshine

## Abstract

Host factors determine pathogen tropism but knowledge of host genes facilitating enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) infection is limited. To identify host determinants required for infection by EPEC, we performed two independent genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screens. Both converged on host N-glycosylation as a critical requirement for infection. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of N-glycan maturation revealed that N-glycosylation promotes infection through two distinct pathways. First, N-linked poly-N-acetyllactosamine glycans serve as receptors for the major EPEC adhesin, the bundle-forming pilus (BFP). Second, perturbation of N-glycosylation compromises host membrane structure, resulting in reduced type III secretion system activity, independently of host cell attachment. Using epithelial monolayers derived from human colon and jejunum organoids, we further show that EPEC attachment inversely correlates with terminal mannose exposure, suggesting glycan composition may be involved in determining intestinal tropism. Together, these findings establish host N-glycan maturation as a key host pathway exploited during enteric infection.

## Abstract

Cohen Yaron et al. identify host N-glycan maturation as a key determinant of efficient enteropathogenic E. coli infection through two genome-wide screens. Complex N-glycans promote bacterial attachment and regulate effector delivery through both attachment-dependent and attachment-independent mechanisms.

## Introduction

Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) causes infantile diarrhea, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.1 The disease can be severe and sometimes fatal,2 occurring in both outbreaks and sporadic cases.3 EPEC belongs to a group of pathogens that induce “attaching and effacing” (AE) lesions in the intestinal epithelium, characterized by microvilli effacement, intimate bacterial adherence, and the formation of actin-rich “pedestals” beneath attached bacteria.1 EPEC infection progresses through a multistep process involving extensive cross-talk between bacterial and host factors. Initial attachment is mediated by bundle-forming pili (BFPs), a type IV pilus that promotes microcolony formation and adherence.4 After attachment, EPEC deploys its primary virulence factor, the type III secretion system (T3SS), a syringe-like apparatus composed of more than 20 proteins.5 Through the T3SS, EPEC injects effector proteins that disrupt host processes such as cytoskeletal organization, vesicular trafficking, signal transduction, and cell cycle control.6

Tir is the first T3SS effector EPEC injects into the host cell.7 Once translocated, Tir rapidly assumes a hairpin-like structure within the host membrane, with both its N- and C-termini localized to the host cell cytoplasm and a surface-exposed loop.8 This loop then serves as a binding site for the EPEC outer membrane protein intimin, resulting in intimate bacterial attachment to the host cell.8 In parallel, the C-terminal of translocated Tir recruits and activates actin polymerization factors, including N-WASP and the downstream Arp2/3 complex, resulting in the formation of actin structures beneath the attached bacteria, termed pedestals.9 Additional injected effectors include both pro- and anti-cytotoxicity factors. The pro-cytotoxic effectors include Map, EspF, NleH, and Tir,6 whereas effectors that protect against cytotoxicity include NleB, NleD, NleF, EspL, and EspZ.6,10 We recently showed that EPEC overexpressing the small RNA (sRNA) MgrR (Mg²⁺-responsive RNA) becomes hypertoxic to infected cells.11 This effect is mediated, at least in part, by MgrR-dependent inhibition of CesT production. CesT is a chaperone required for the translocation of several pro- and anti-cytotoxic effectors, such as Tir and EspZ.11,12 Thus, by repressing CesT, MgrR induces imbalance between the two opposite activities, leading to pronounced increase in the cytotoxic potential of EPEC.11

Many aspects of EPEC-host crosstalk remain unknown. For example, how the T3SS translocon channel is inserted into the host cell membrane, how this channel insertion stimulates effector translocation, and how effectors such as Tir and EspZ are themselves inserted into the host membrane to become transmembrane proteins. At least some of these processes are likely to require host factors. To identify such host factors, here we describe the design of two independent CRISPR-based functional genomic screens. One screen is based on host cell cytotoxicity, and the other on Tir-intimin interaction. These screens identified multiple host pathways, including the actin cytoskeleton structure (e.g., the Arp2/3 complex, spectrin, and AIF1L), genes involved in gene expression regulation such as KMT2D, YTHDF2, and ZNF619, and genes involved in glycosylation. Since multiple genes required for the poly-N-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc) glycosylation pathway emerged among the top hits in both screens, here we investigated this pathway and identified it as a critical determinant of EPEC infectivity. We found that LacNAc glycosylation is required for both BFP-mediated attachment and efficient T3SS effector translocation activity. Furthermore, infecting colon- and jejunum-derived human organoids showed a correlation between preferential jejunum attachment and the surface glycans displayed on this tissue. Together, our study highlights the complex role of N-glycosylation in EPEC infection and provides the foundation for future investigations into anti-virulence strategies against diarrheal disease.

## Results

### Two CRISPR screens identify host N-glycosylation as a central requirement for EPEC infection

To identify host factors required for EPEC infection, we performed two independent genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screens that interrogate distinct stages of the infection process. One screen was based on EPEC cytotoxicity toward HT-29 cells, derived from colorectal adenocarcinoma. To perform the screen, we generated a population of HT-29 cells with mutations across most of the known human genes, using the Avana guide RNA (gRNA) CRISPR library.13 To improve the screen efficiency, we employed a hyper-toxic EPEC variant containing a plasmid overexpressing the sRNA MgrR (EPEC/pMgrR), which enhances its cytotoxicity.11 The mutated HT-29 cells14 were infected with EPEC/pMgrR, and the ∼10% of the cells that survived the infection were cured of bacteria, expanded, and subjected to a second infection cycle (Figure 1A). After four enrichment cycles, gRNAs from the surviving population were amplified and their relative abundance was compared with gRNAs from the initial cell library. For the second screen, we developed an assay for staining host cells that present translocated Tir on their surface, indicating protein translocation by infecting EPEC. We infected host cells with an EPEC Δeae mutant (i.e., intimin−, Tir+, strain CX2168), which rapidly attaches to the host cells via its BFP and injects Tir but cannot bind to the translocated Tir due to the lack of intimin. Infected cells displaying translocated Tir on their surface were then “labeled” employing E. coli K12 harboring a plasmid encoding intimin and GFP (pNE8145). These GFP-expressing bacteria decorate specifically cells displaying the surface-exposed loop of Tir through the expressed intimin (Figure S1A). We optimized this assay for a fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based screen using suspension-growing K562 cells as the host. This cell line, although derived from chronic myelogenous leukemia, was found to be well-suited for the assay as infection with EPEC led to characteristic actin accumulation at sites of bacterial contact (Figure S1B). Moreover, infection with EPEC Δeae enabled Tir-dependent binding of E. coli K12 expressing intimin and GFP, yielding a high signal/noise ratio (Figures S1C and S1D). To perform the screen, we similarly generated a population of mutant K562 cells using the Brunello gRNA CRISPR library.13 These mutated cells were subjected to Tir-intimin based “labeling” screen, involving infection with EPEC Δeae, incubation with E. coli K12 expressing intimin and GFP, followed by fixation and sorting for the 5%–7% brightest and darkest cells (Figures 1B and S1E). We then compared the gRNA representation between these low- and high-GFP populations. Cells in which genes required for EPEC infection were disrupted should lack surface Tir and thus fail to be labeled, resulting in an over-representation of their corresponding gRNAs in the low-GFP group. This analysis revealed significantly enriched genes (Figure 1D; Table S2), representing putative host factors required for Tir translocation to the host cell membrane.

For downstream analysis, the top 20 hits from each screen were grouped into four functional categories: (1) glycan biosynthesis and processing, (2) actin-related, including components of the Arp2/3 complex, (3) gene expression regulation, and (4) cellular metabolism and homeostasis (Table 1; Tables S3 and S4). Notably, among the top hits identified in both screens were B3GNT2, encoding a β-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase, which is required for the synthesis of poly-LacNAc chains.16 Additional high-ranking hits from the cytotoxicity screen included MGAT1, which initiates complex N-glycan branching,16 SLC35A2, which transports uridine diphosphate galactose (UDP-galactose) into the Golgi lumen where galactosyltransferases add galactose to N-glycans,17 and TMEM165, a Golgi Mn2+/Ca2+ transporter that regulates the manganese supply required for N-glycosylation enzymes.18 Moreover, several additional genes involved in LacNAc biosynthesis, including MGAT2 and MGAT5, were also identified, although they did not rank among the top 20 hits (Table S1). ### MGAT1 knockout cells display increased resistance to EPEC toxicity

To achieve complete loss of N-LacNAc glycosylation, we targeted MGAT1, which catalyzes the addition of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) to mannose residues on N-glycoproteins,16 a prerequisite for the generation of N-linked poly-LacNAc (Figure 2A). We used HeLa cells for this knock-out because they are better than HT-29 and K562 for immunofluorescence microscopy analyses. Disruption of the MGAT1 gene was confirmed by sequencing of the gRNA-targeted region (Figure S2A), whereas the absence of MGAT1 protein was confirmed by both western blotting and immunofluorescence microscopy using a monoclonal anti-MGAT1 antibody (Figures S2B and S2C). To assess whether MGAT1 affects host susceptibility to EPEC-induced cell death, wild-type (WT) and MGAT1 knockout (KO) HeLa cells were infected with EPEC/pMgrR, and toxicity was assessed by quantification of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) released to the medium by dying host cells. In WT HeLa cells, infection resulted in approximately 70% cytotoxicity, whereas MGAT1 KO cells showed only ∼35% cytotoxicity (Figure 2B). ### MGAT1 KO alters cell surface glycan structures

Since MGAT1 catalyzes the addition of GlcNAc to mannose, disruption of MGAT1 is expected to eliminate LacNAc structures, while simultaneously increasing the display of terminal mannose residues on the cell surface (Figure 2A). To assess alterations in surface glycosylation, we stained WT and MGAT1 KO cells with fluorescently labeled concanavalin A (ConA), which preferentially binds mannose residues, and wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), which binds primarily GlcNAc.19 Flow cytometry analysis showed that MGAT1 KO cells exhibited a marked increase in ConA binding and a corresponding decrease in WGA staining compared to WT cells (Figure 2C). To visualize this at the single-cell level, we mixed WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells in a 1:1 ratio and performed dual staining with anti-MGAT1 antibodies and with ConA. KO cells, lacking perinuclear MGAT1 signal, displayed significantly higher ConA staining, confirming increased surface exposure of mannose residues in MGAT1-deficient cells (Figure 2D). These results point to a possible role of surface glycans in EPEC infection.

### Reduced attachment of EPEC microcolonies to MGAT1 KO cells

To test for the role of N-glycosylation in EPEC attachment, a 1:1 mixture of WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells was infected with EPEC wild-type. The infected cells were fixed at different time points post-infection and stained with anti-MGAT1 antibody to differentiate HeLa WT from MGAT1 KO cells. Reduced attachment of EPEC-microcolonies to MGAT1 KO cells was evident at 1–1.5 h post-infection (Figure 3A). For attachment quantification we used similar microscopy of infected monocultures of either WT HeLa or MGAT1 KO cells (Figure 3B). Attachment to the MGAT1 KO cells was restored upon ectopic expression of MGAT1 (Figure S2A). Differences in EPEC attachment to WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells were less pronounced at 2–2.5 h post-infection (Figures 3A and 3B). This timeline aligns with initial MGAT1-dependent attachment mediated by BFP at ∼1.5 h post-infection, followed by T3SS maturation at ∼2 h post-infection, which leads to Tir/intimin-mediated attachment.20 To test this prediction, we infected the host cells with a T3SS-deficient EPEC strain (ΔescRSTU, RP7457), which attaches to host cells exclusively via BFP. We found that attachment of this mutant to MGAT1 KO cells remained low even at 2 h post-infection (Figures 3C and 3D) and was restored upon complementation with ectopic MGAT1 (Figure S3A). To test whether the reduced attachment is related to the lack of surface glycans with terminal LacNAc or to changes in the surface proteome, we attempted to inhibit EPEC attachment by adding exogenous soluble LacNAc. We found that this treatment inhibited EPEC attachment to WT HeLa cells to a level similar to the one observed in MGAT1 KO cells without external inhibition (Figures 3E and 3F). These results suggest that the reduced attachment of EPEC microcolonies to the MGAT1 KO cells is due to the absence of surface-exposed terminal LacNAc and is not directly related to variation in the surface proteome. These results strongly support previous suggestions that LacNAc serves as the BFP receptor.21,22

### Inverse attachment of BFP and type I fimbriae to WT and MGAT1 KO cells

To further explore whether the reduction in EPEC attachment to MGAT1 KO cells was specific to BFP-mediated attachment, we assessed attachment of a BFP-deficient EPEC strain (ΔbfpA, RP7404) to WT and MGAT1 KO cells. During these experiments, we observed substantial variation in attachment among cultures initiated from individual, well-isolated ΔbfpA colonies picked from agar plates. Attachment of these cultures to MGAT1 KO cells exhibited a bimodal distribution (Figures 4A and 4B), with either minimal attachment (e.g., colony 2, Figures 4A and 4B), or extensive attachment (e.g., colony 1, Figures 4A and 4B). In contrast, the attachment of the ΔbfpA mutant to WT host cells was found to be consistently low (Figures 4A and 4B). Since MGAT1 deletion exposes terminal mannose residues (Figures 2A and 2C), we hypothesized that this bimodality reflects phase variation in the expression of the type I fimbriae (T1F), a mannose-binding adhesin.23,24 We thus used PCR to determine the phase state in EPEC ΔbfpA cultures originated from well-isolated colonies and correlated it to attachment of the bacteria in the corresponding cultures to MGAT1 KO cells. We found a strong correlation between T1F-ON state and extensive attachment to the MGAT1 KO cells (Figure 4C), consistent with the idea that T1F expression promotes binding to the mannose-enriched surface of the MGAT1 KO cells. Furthermore, ectopic expression of MGAT1 in the KO cells restored the phenotype of low T1F-mediated binding (Figure S3B), likely due to capping of terminal mannose residues by LacNAc. To further test whether the enhanced attachment was mediated by mannose recognition, we attempted to inhibit EPEC attachment by adding exogenous soluble mannose. The addition of D-mannose had no detectable effect on the attachment of wild-type EPEC to either WT or MGAT1 KO cells, consistent with BFP-mediated binding (Figure S3C). In contrast, D-mannose markedly reduced attachment of the ΔbfpA T1F-ON strain to MGAT1 KO cells, while having little effect on its already low attachment to WT cells (Figure S3D). These findings support the conclusion that mannose-dependent T1F interactions mediate the enhanced attachment of the ΔbfpA T1F-ON strain to MGAT1 KO cells. Collectively, these findings further support the premise that LacNAc serves as a critical receptor for BFP-mediated attachment, and its absence in MGAT1 KO cells impairs EPEC binding. ### MGAT1 enhances T3SS effector translocation via attachment-dependent and -independent mechanisms

To assess whether MGAT1 affects the EPEC T3SS activity, we compared the efficiency of effector translocation into WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells. To determine injection efficacy, we employed the split nanoluciferase assay.25 To this end, we generated stable WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cell lines expressing the nanoluciferase large subunit (LgBit) and engineered two EPEC strains expressing their native EspG or EspF effectors fused to the corresponding small subunit (termed EspG-HiBit and EspF-HiBit). Upon successful delivery of the HiBit-tagged effectors into host cells, reconstitution of active nanoluciferase occurs, resulting in the production of a luminescence signal. This assay showed reduced translocation of EspF and EspG into MGAT1 KO cells (Figures S4A and S4B), which correlates with reduced pedestal formation, a common readout for Tir translocation26 (Figures S4C and S4D). These results confirm that the reduced attachment to MGAT1 KO cells leads to significant reduction in T3SS-mediated protein translocation.

We next examined whether MGAT1 also contributes to T3SS activity through an attachment-independent mechanism. To this aim, we used an EPEC ΔbfpA Δfim double mutant (NY10924), which showed equal, albeit low, binding to WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells (Figures 4D and 4E). ### MGAT1 loss broadly remodels the host cell-surface proteome

N-glycosylation is critical for Golgi-mediated sorting of proteins and trafficking to their final destination, including the cell membrane.27 We therefore asked whether differences in the composition of membrane proteins can explain why T3SS function remained impaired upon infection of MGAT1 KO cells even when attachment was similar. Using cell-surface biotinylation followed by mass spectrometry (MS), we revealed substantial differences between the surface proteomes of WT and MGAT1 KO cells (Figure 5D; Table S5). Among the most strongly depleted proteins in MGAT1 KO cells were those involved in cell adhesion and extracellular interactions, membrane domain organization, and cytoskeletal organization (Figure 5D; Table S6). These include LGALS3 (galectin-3) that cross-links complex N-glycans thus stabilizes these glycoproteins at the surface28; ITGA4, ITGA7 (integrin-α4 and -α7), matrix adhesion receptors that also contribute to raft stabilization through their clustering and scaffolding29,30,31; ICAM1, MCAM, and BCAM that mediate cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions; and CAVIN1, the caveolae-associated scaffolding protein that is essential together with LGALS3, for caveolae biogenesis.32 These observations suggest that MGAT1 loss broadly compromises the integrity of host cell membrane microdomains, which were reported to be required for insertion of the EPEC T3SS translocon.33,34 Furthermore, we found that the membrane-associated levels of several top hits from our CRISPR screen including ARPC4 (Arp2/3 complex), SPTBN1 (spectrin), and CTNND1 (p120-catenin), were also reduced in MGAT1 KO cells (Table S3; Figure 5D), which might also contribute to the reduced T3SS activity.

### Lectin heterogeneity in human intestinal organoids correlates with EPEC attachment

## Discussion

Using two independent host-targeted genetic screens, we identified factors required for EPEC infection. Notably, genes essential for the poly-LacNAc N-glycosylation pathway were among the top hits in both screens. Further investigation revealed that LacNAc is essential for host attachment through BFP, substantially extending and strengthening previous observations.21 Disruption of the LacNAc biosynthesis pathway resulted in exposure of terminal mannose residues on the host cell surface, which strongly promoted the attachment and expansion of EPEC phase-variants expressing mannose-binding T1F. Thus, when LacNAc-mediated attachment is impaired, EPEC can compensate by upregulating T1F. In addition to altered glycan presentation, perturbation of the N-glycosylation pathway induced broad changes in the host cell-surface proteome, reflecting the role of N-glycosylation in protein sorting within the Golgi.27 These alterations of the host proteome correlated with reduced T3SS effector delivery by the infecting bacteria, potentially due to the loss of a host surface factor required for optimal T3SS docking. Finally, using human intestinal organoids, we provide evidence that variability in cell surface glycosylation within the human intestine may contribute to EPEC tissue tropism.

The importance of BFP for infection has been highlighted in clinical studies. A human experimental infection trial using bfpA mutants and the BFP regulator perA mutants showed significantly fewer symptoms in volunteers infected with the mutant bacteria compared to those infected with the wild-type strain.37 In recent years, the prevalence of atypical EPEC, which lack BFP, has increased38,39,40,41 but these strains are associated with less severe disease. In a study analyzing 70 isolates from patients with varying disease severities, lethal cases were exclusively associated with typical EPEC strains expressing BFP.42 Our results and earlier reports demonstrated that soluble LacNAc, or LacNAc conjugated to bovine serum albumin, can inhibit BFP-dependent adherence to epithelial cell lines or human biopsies,22 making LacNAc, or a mix of LacNAc and mannose, a potential inhibitor to treat EPEC infection.

Our findings suggest that, in addition to forming receptors for EPEC attachment, N-glycosylation supports EPEC infection by regulating the membrane-associated proteome and thus maintaining the host membrane’s functional landscape. We speculate that depletion of CAVIN1, integrins, and galectin-3 in MGAT1 KO cells leads to global collapse of specialized membrane microdomains28 providing a plausible mechanistic explanation for reduced T3SS effector delivery by EPEC upon infection. This aligns with reports that translocon insertion requires a defined lipid-protein environment.33,34 The surface proteome results suggest that N-glycosylation further contributes to EPEC infection by regulating the membrane association of host factors emerged in our CRISPR screen, as required for EPEC toxicity, including Arp2/3 complex subunits (e.g., ARPC4) and cytoskeletal linkers (SPTBN1 and CTNND1). Finally, we cannot exclude an additional scenario, where a specific N-glycosylated protein is required for EPEC T3SS activity, as exemplified in the case of the Vibrio parahaemolyticus T3SS2, where translocon insertion requires fucosylated glycans on the host cell surface.14

EPEC preferentially colonizes the infant’s small intestine, yet the underlying mechanisms of this tropism are only partially understood. Several factors likely influence tissue specificity, including nutrient availability, interactions with commensal microbiota, local immune responses, and the pathogen’s ability to attach to host cells, particularly through recognition of LacNAc structures. Although the N-glycosylation landscape of the human intestine is not fully characterized, studies using Caco-2 cells have shown that undifferentiated cells are enriched in mannose residues, whereas differentiated cells display more complex glycans.43 These insights prompted us to investigate whether similar differences exist across cell types in human intestinal organoids. Lectin staining using ConA, which binds preferentially to mannose residues but not to LacNAc, revealed higher staining intensity in colon organoids compared to jejunum organoids, indicating a relative abundance of mannose-rich glycans and reduced terminal LacNAc structures in the colon epithelium. Consistent with this, EPEC attachment was markedly reduced in colon organoid monolayers. Furthermore, the few EPEC microcolonies that did adhere to the colon-derived monolayers were localized to regions with faint ConA staining, suggesting these areas contained more complex glycans. These findings suggest that the higher abundance of complex glycans in the jejunum epithelium may contribute to the preferential colonization of the small intestine by EPEC.

While BFP expression is promoted by the PerA encoded on the perABC operon,44 PerC has been shown to bias the T1F phase switch toward the OFF state,45 suggesting that expression of these adhesins may be inversely coordinated. Consistent with this model, all 12 independently isolated EPEC wild-type colonies examined in the present study were in the T1F-OFF state under the infection conditions used. Thus, the organoid attachment patterns are most consistent with BFP-mediated recognition of LacNAc-containing glycans rather than T1F-dependent binding. The mechanism of the proposed coordinated regulation of BFP and T1F warrants further investigation.

Beyond glycosylation, the prominence of actin-regulatory genes in our screens underscores the complex role of host actin cytoskeleton in supporting infection. Most of the Arp2/3-complex components, alongside its two upstream regulators CDC42 and WASL (N-WASP), were prominently enriched in the toxicity-based screen. These factors are central mediators of actin pedestal formation downstream of Tir-intimin engagement and have previously been implicated in EPEC- and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC)-induced cytoskeletal remodeling and toxicity.46,47,48,49,50 The Tir-translocation screen identified additional actin-associated proteins such as ACTR10 and AIF1L, with the latter previously reported to be associated with actin rearrangement mediated by the T3SS of Shigella.51 Additionally, it remains to be elucidated if and how these factors might enhance Tir translocation. Additional groups of significant and interesting hits identified in the screens encompassed genes involved in gene expression regulation and cellular metabolism and homeostasis, including transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulators such as KMT2D and ZNF619, and kinases such as STK11 and STK17B. The specific mechanistic roles of these genes and encoded proteins remain to be first validated and then elucidated.

Overall, our results establish host N-glycosylation as a central determinant of EPEC infection. Beyond confirming its role in bacterial adhesion, this work reveals that N-glycosylation is essential for efficient T3SS effector delivery and is potentially involved in EPEC tropism to the small intestine. These insights expand our understanding of host-pathogen interactions and open new avenues for targeting host glycosylation pathways to modulate bacterial virulence.

### Limitations of the study

This study was performed using cultured epithelial cells and human intestinal organoids, which do not fully recapitulate the complexity of the intestinal environment. Therefore, the contribution of host N-glycosylation to EPEC infection and tissue tropism remains challenging, given the lack of robust animal model for EPEC infection.

### Method details

#### Cell culture

HeLa, HEK293T, and HT-29 cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM; Sartorius) supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS; Gibco) and penicillin-streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. K562 cells were maintained in RPMI 1640 (Sartorius) supplemented with 10% FCS and penicillin-streptomycin under the same conditions.

Where indicated, cells were supplemented with 200 μM N-acetyl-D-lactosamine (LacNAc; Sigma-Aldrich) or 10% D-mannose (Calbiochem) at the time of infection. For kifunensine treatment, HeLa cells were cultured in the presence or absence of 5 μM kifunensine for 48 h before infection and then seeded into the appropriate culture vessels for each experiment. HT-29 cells were treated with kifunensine for 4–5 days before infection.

#### Construction of MGAT1 KO cells

MGAT1 knockout (MGAT1 KO) HeLa cells were generated using the CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing system. An sgRNA targeting MGAT1 (5′-AGTCCTGGCTAACGATGATG-3′) was designed as previously described55 and cloned into pSpCas9(BB)-2A-Puro (PX459) v2.0 (Addgene plasmid #62988). Successful cloning was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. HeLa cells were transfected with the PX459-MGAT1 sgRNA plasmid using Transporter 5 Transfection Reagent (Polysciences) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, plasmid DNA was mixed with 150 mM NaCl and Transporter 5, incubated for 30 min at room temperature, and added to the cells. Five hours later, the transfection medium was replaced with fresh growth medium. One day after transfection, puromycin (2 μg/mL) was added to select for transfected cells. Forty-eight hours after transfection, puromycin was removed, and surviving cells were diluted to approximately one cell per well in 96-well plates to obtain single-cell-derived clones. Individual clones were screened by Sanger sequencing, western blotting, and immunofluorescence microscopy. A clone carrying a biallelic MGAT1 knockout that exhibited normal morphology and growth characteristics was selected for all subsequent experiments. For complementation experiments, MGAT1 KO cells were transfected with a plasmid expressing MGAT1-GFP or GFP alone as a control. Twenty-four hours after transfection, the cells were reseeded for infection.

#### Plasmid construction

The pNE8145 plasmid generated in this study is listed in the key resources table. DNA fragments were amplified by PCR using primers listed in Table S7 and assembled using Gibson Assembly Master Mix (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The assembled plasmid was introduced into Escherichia coli MG1655 by electroporation, purified using a plasmid miniprep kit, and verified by Sanger sequencing prior to use.

#### Construction of bacterial strains

EPEC mutant strains are derivatives of the WT strain E2348/69. Mutants were constructed by homology recombination using the λ Red system as described.53 Desired DNA fragments with homology sequences were created by PCR with the primers listed in Table S7 and Gibson assembly as needed. Scar-less deletions were similarly constructed using λ Red system and tet-sacB cassette as described.56 Mutations were verified using PCR and sequencing.

#### Generation of stable LgBit-expressing cell lines

Stable LgBit-expressing HeLa, MGAT1 KO, and HT-29 cell lines were generated by lentiviral transduction. Lentiviral particles were produced by co-transfecting HEK293T cells with pLVX-EF1α-LgBit-IRES-Puro, psPAX2, and pMD2.G using Transporter 5 Transfection Reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Lentiviral supernatants were collected at 48 and 72 h after transfection, concentrated by polyethylene glycol 8000 (PEG8000) precipitation, and used to transduce the indicated cell lines. Transduced cells were selected with 2 μg/mL puromycin to generate stable LgBit-expressing cell lines.

#### Bacterial growth conditions and infection

A single colony of EPEC was inoculated into 2 mL LB medium supplemented with the appropriate antibiotic (100 μg/mL ampicillin, 50 μg/mL streptomycin, 25 μg/mL chloramphenicol, or 40 μg/mL kanamycin). Unless otherwise indicated, mammalian cells were seeded to approximately 70% confluency prior to infection. Bacteria were cultured overnight at 37 °C without shaking (OD600 ∼1). Cells were washed twice with PBS and antibiotic-free DMEM was added. Bacteria were added to mammalian cells at the multiplicity of infection (MOI) of approximately 100:1, and infections were carried out for 1 to 3.5 h as indicated. For GFP, mCherry, or mScarlet expression in the bacteria, appropriate concentration of IPTG (isopropyl-D-thiogalactopyranoside, Sigma) was added.

#### Genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 toxicity screen

HT-29-Cas9 CRISPR libraries were constructed as described previously14 using the Avana sgRNA library, which contains four different sgRNAs targeting each human protein-coding gene.13 Two T225 flasks were seeded with 40 × 106 cells per flask and then incubated for 24 h. At the time of the screen, there were ∼80 × 106 cells, corresponding to ∼1000x coverage per sgRNA. Cells were at ∼80–90% confluence at the time of infection. The infection was performed as described above with minor modifications. Briefly, HT-29 libraries were infected with pre-activated EPEC/pMgrR at a MOI of 100 for 90 min. After infection, the libraries were expanded in McCoy’s 5A + FBS containing 50 μg/mL gentamicin. Flasks were checked daily to monitor recovery of survivor cells; when 80–90% confluency was achieved, cells were trypsinized, pooled, and reseeded for the next round of infection. In total, four rounds of infection were conducted.

To sequence the CRISPR libraries, gDNA was prepared with the GeneGet DNA purification kit from ∼10 × 106 cells. sgRNA sequences were amplified as previously performed57 and sequenced for 78 cycles with a MiSeq V3 150-cycle kit to a depth of 0.4–2.7 million reads/sample. Fastq files were trimmed in CLC Genomics Workbench and then mapped with MaGeCk.15 Comparisons between input and output libraries were performed using the -test command, and control non-targeting guide RNAs were used for normalization.

#### Genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 Tir translocation screen

K562 cells were transduced with the Human sgRNA library Brunello in lentiCRISPRv2 (Addgene #73179-LV) with MOI of 0.3. Two days later, transduced cells were selected for 4 days with 1 μg/mL puromycin, after which a fraction of cells was collected for analysis of the initial sgRNA pool.

For the screen, approximately 1.3 × 108 pooled knockout cells were cultured in antibiotic-free RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FCS, maintaining approximately 1,600-fold sgRNA coverage. Pre-activated cultures of EPEC Δeae and EPEC Δtir were prepared by dilution into RPMI and incubation for 3 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2 without shaking. In parallel, MC1061/pNE8145, which provided the highest signal-to-noise ratio, was grown in LB medium with shaking (160 rpm) to an OD600 of 0.3–0.4 and transferred to RPMI before infection.

The K562 mutant library was incubated with pre-activated EPEC Δeae or EPEC Δtir for 1 h, washed once with PBS, and subsequently incubated with MC1061/pNE8145 for an additional 30 min. Cells were then washed, fixed with 2% formaldehyde for 10 min, washed with TBS followed by cold PBS, resuspended in cold PBS containing 2% FCS, and stored overnight at 4 °C protected from light.

The following day, cells infected with EPEC Δeae were analyzed and sorted by flow cytometry (Sony) according to their associated GFP signal. Cell populations with the highest and lowest GFP intensities (approximately the upper and lower 5%; ∼5 × 106 cells each) were collected. Genomic DNA was isolated using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN), and sgRNA sequences were amplified by PCR and sequenced on a NextSeq 500 (Illumina). The screen was performed in three independent biological replicates. Gene enrichment analysis was performed using MAGeCK by comparing the low-GFP and high-GFP populations across all three replicates. The final top 20 hits were selected based on a combination of MAGeCK RRA significance (FDR <0.05), a median Log2 Fold Change >1.5; and a requirement for substantial raw read counts (>100 normalized reads) in at least one experimental replicate, prioritizing genes with high biological signal-to-noise ratios.

#### Cytotoxicity LDH assay

Cells were infected with EPEC/pMgrR as described above for 3.5 h. Following infection, culture supernatants were collected, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release was quantified using the LDH Cytotoxicity Assay Kit (Fluorometric; Abcam) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Fluorescence was measured in 96-well plates using a Spark 10M microplate reader (TECAN).

#### Split NanoLuc effector translocation assay

Effector translocation was quantified using the split NanoLuc luciferase assay as previously described25 with minor modifications. LgBit-expressing cells were seeded in white 96-well plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and grown to approximately 80% confluency. EPEC strains expressing EspF-HiBit or EspG-HiBit were cultured overnight as described above. For infection, 10 μL of the overnight bacterial culture was diluted in 1 mL phenol red-free DMEM, and 100 μL of the bacterial suspension was added to cells following two washes with PBS.

Immediately after infection, 20 μL of Nano-Glo Live Cell reagent (Promega) was added to each well. The reagent consisted of 1 μL cell-permeable luciferase substrate, 0.1 μL DrkBiT peptide, and 18.9 μL Live Cell Substrate (LCS) buffer (Promega). Luminescence was measured every 15 min using a Spark 10M microplate reader (TECAN) pre-equilibrated to 37 °C. To account for differences in cell number, luminescence values were normalized to the initial residual LgBit signal measured in each well before HiBit-dependent signal development (Figure S7).

#### Flow cytometry

HeLa and K562 cells were infected and/or treated as indicated. Following infection, HeLa cells were detached by scraping in PBS, whereas K562 cells were collected by centrifugation and resuspended in PBS. Cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde in PBS for 10 min, washed with PBS (300×g, 5 min), and, where indicated, stained with fluorescent lectins for 15 min followed by PBS washes. Cells were then resuspended in PBS and analyzed using a CytoFLEX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter). Flow cytometry data were analyzed using CytExpert (Beckman Coulter), FlowJo (BD Biosciences), or Floreada.io.

#### Immunofluorescence microscopy

Following infection, cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde in PBS for 10 min at room temperature, washed with PBS, and processed for fluorescence microscopy. For immunostaining, cells were permeabilized with 0.25% Triton X-100 in TBS for 10 min, washed twice with PBS, and blocked with 2% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in TBS for 1 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. Cells were then incubated with primary anti-MGAT1 or rabbit anti-EPEC antibodies for 30–60 min at room temperature, washed three times with PBS, and incubated for 1 h with the appropriate fluorescent secondary antibodies together with DAPI and either rhodamine-phalloidin or Alexa Fluor 350-phalloidin.

For lectin staining, fixed cells were incubated with Concanavalin A (ConA)-Alexa Fluor 488 or wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-FITC for 15 min, followed by three PBS washes. When lectin staining was combined with MGAT1 immunostaining, cells were permeabilized only after completion of the lectin staining to prevent intracellular lectin labeling.

For microscopy of infected K562 cells, cells were collected by centrifugation during washing steps and, following fixation, were centrifuged onto coverslips before staining.

Images were acquired using an Axio Observer Z1 inverted fluorescence microscope (Zeiss) equipped with a Prime BSI camera (Photometrics). Image acquisition and processing were performed using ZEN Pro 2012 software (Zeiss).

#### Semi-quantitative PCR for T1F phase-state determination

Bacterial colonies or overnight cultures were lysed by boiling at 95 °C for 10 min in distilled water and clarified by centrifugation. Two microliters of the lysate were used as a template for 20 cycles of PCR with primers specific for the ON and OFF orientations of the type 1 fimbriae (T1F) phase switch.

#### Cell surface proteomics

Surface proteins from four independent biological replicates of WT and MGAT1 KO HeLa cells were selectively labeled using a membrane-impermeable sulfo-NHS-biotin (EZ-Link Sulfo-NHS-Biotin, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were cultured in 6-well plates to ∼90% confluence. Following two washes with ice-cold PBS, cells were incubated on ice for 1 h with Sulfo-NHS-SS-Biotin or PBS for negative control. Excess NHS-biotin was quenched by two sequential washes with TBS, followed by one additional wash with cold PBS. Cells were then scraped from the plate and lysed in 1% Triton X-100 and biotinylated proteins were enriched by incubating the lysate with streptavidin-agarose beads for 1 h at RT with gentle rotation. Beads were washed extensively with PBS and subjected to proteolysis and mass spectrometry (MS) analysis.

Proteolysis and LC-MS/MS were done by the Smoler Proteomics Center at the Israel Institute of Technology. Briefly, beads were washed and subjected to on-bead digestion in 2 M urea, 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate with reduction (10 mM DTT, 60 °C, 30 min) and alkylation (10 mM iodoacetamide, 30 min, dark). Proteins were digested overnight at 37 °C with modified trypsin (Promega), followed by a second 4 h digestion. Peptides were desalted using Oasis HLB μElution plates, dried, and re-suspended in 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile.

Peptides were analyzed by LC-MS/MS on a Q Exactive HF-X coupled to an Ultimate 3000 UHPLC. Samples were loaded onto a 30-cm C18 column and eluted using a 5–28% acetonitrile gradient over 60 min, followed by column washing. MS1 scans were acquired at 60,000 resolution (m/z 300–1500) and MS2 scans at 15,000 resolution using HCD (NCE 27). Dynamic exclusion was set to 20 s.

MS Data Analysis: Raw data were processed in MaxQuant (v2.1.3.0) with the Andromeda search engine against the human UniProt database, using standard parameters (Cys carbamidomethylation; Met oxidation and N-terminal acetylation as variable modifications; 1% FDR at peptide/protein level; minimum 7 aa; up to two missed cleavages).

Label-free quantification was performed using MaxLFQ49, and statistical analyses were carried out in Perseus.58,59 The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE60 partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD083032.

#### Human intestinal organoids

Patient-derived colonic and jejunal organoid lines were retrieved from an established biobank,36,61 generated from patients who underwent surgical resection at the University Hospital of Würzburg. The study was approved by the ethical committee of the University of Würzburg (Approval 37/16), informed consent was obtained from all donors, and the study methodologies conform to the standards set by the Declaration of Helsinki.

Organoids were cultured in domes of Matrigel (Corning) overlayed with expansion medium (Advanced DMEM/F12 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 10 mM HEPES (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 10 mM nicotinamide (Sigma-Aldrich); 10 μM SB202190 (Sigma-Aldrich); 1x B27 supplement (Invitrogen); 10 nM [Leu15]-Gastrin I (Sigma-Aldrich); 50 ng/mL human recombinant EGF (Peprotech); 500 nM A-83-01 (Tocris); 1 mM N-Acetylcysteine (Sigma-Aldrich); primocin (Invitrogen, ant-pm-1), in a humidified incubator at 37 °C and 5% CO2.

Organoids were passaged every 9–12 days at a ratio 1:2 to 1:5 depending on the donor and the medium was changed every 2–3 days. In the first two days passaging, 10 μM ROCK inhibitor (AbMole Bioscience) was included in the medium.

2D monolayers in 48-well plates were generated according to previously established protocols36: organoids were dissociated into single cells using TrypLE (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 10 min at 37 °C, seeded into the 48-well plate and grown in the above-described organoid culture medium at 37 °C and 5% CO2. Primocin and 10 μM ROCK inhibitor were kept for the first 1–2 days of culture.

For infection, EPEC cultures were prepared as described above with the following modifications. Overnight culture was diluted 1:100 the next day in DMEM with 1% GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For GFP expression, IPTG (Sigma) was added 2 h after the start of the day culture to a final concentration of 10 mM. When OD600 = 0.15–0.25 was reached, bacteria were added to the respective monolayers at an MOI of 10. Infection was stopped at 3 h p.i. by washing the monolayers thoroughly with PBS followed by fixation with 4% PFA (Sigma).

Fixed organoid-derived monolayers were blocked with 1% BSA (Serva) for at least 30 min at RT and stained for Concanavalin A (ConA)-Alexa 647 (Invitrogen) at a final concentration of 50 μg/mL for 30 min at RT. Monolayers were imaged on a DMi8 Leica fluorescent microscope.

To quantify ConA staining heterogeneity, 20× images were analyzed in a blinded manner. Cells were manually classified as ConA-high or ConA-low, and their percentages were calculated. A custom macro was used to quantify the total ConA fluorescence intensity and the total number of EPEC microcolonies per image. Microcolonies associated with ConA-high cells were quantified manually.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

For microscopy experiments with cell lines, a two-tailed independent samples t test was conducted using Excel to compare the means of the two groups. The analysis assumed equal variances for both groups and the null hypothesis tested whether there was no significant difference between the group means. n = 100 cells from at least 6 fields per cell line for each condition tested in 2–5 biological replicates. The exact number of biological repeats in each experiment is indicated in the figure legends. For flow cytometry experiments at least 10,000 cells per cell line for each condition were analyzed. For organoid experiments, each biological replicate consisted of an independent patient-derived organoid line and/or an independently repeated experiment performed using organoids at different passages. At least 10 technical replicate images were acquired per condition within each biological replicate. Technical replicate measurements were averaged prior to statistical analysis, and the resulting biological replicate means were used for statistical testing. Individual technical replicate measurements are shown in the graphs to illustrate data distribution. Statistical significance was assessed using Welch’s t test. ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001.
